Newly hatched Common nighthawk chicks emerge after an incubation period of 19 days [ab = 19 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], which corresponds to the optimal artificial incubation conditions established for several caprimulgid species. At hatching, the wet weight at birth of these altricial nestlings is a mere 5.4 grams [Wwb = 5.4 grams], a value consistent with the modest initial masses reported for other aerial insectivores that produce relatively small clutches. This initial investment in neonatal mass, while low in absolute terms, is closely tied to the species' reproductive strategy, which relies on rapid post-hatching growth fueled by intensive biparental provisioning. The chicks are covered in downy feathers at emergence and depend entirely on their parents for thermoregulation and food delivery during the first days of life. Brooding and feeding behaviors are especially critical during the first week, as the nestlings have limited locomotor capabilities and must quickly accumulate somatic tissue to support feather development and the eventual transition to flight.

Chicks that are reared under the thermal conditions typical of the species' active metabolic range at 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C] fledge, achieving their first sustained flight and attaining nutritional independence, at 18 days after hatching [tx = 18 days after hatching]. This relatively rapid fledging period is characteristic of many caprimulgids and allows young to leave the exposed ground nest before predators become a significant threat. Upon fledging, the young birds are still relatively undeveloped and continue to be fed by adults for a short period, but they are capable of short foraging flights. By this stage, the chicks have undergone a marked transformation, transitioning from a downy, sedentary state to a fully feathered, volant form. The post-fledging period is a vulnerable window during which mortality from starvation and predation is high, and the ability to achieve early flight is therefore a critical adaptation shaped by selection pressures related to nest predation and resource availability.

Sexual maturation in the Common nighthawk occurs relatively early in its life history, and under the same active thermal conditions of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], the time since birth at puberty is 54 days [tp = 54 days]. This rapid progression to reproductive capability, measured from the moment of hatching, stands in contrast to the slower maturation schedules observed in many larger-bodied bird species and reflects the nighthawk's life-history strategy as a relatively short-lived, high-fecundity aerial insectivore. The attainment of gonadal maturity at this age allows young-of-the-year to potentially breed in their first summer, although in practice, resource acquisition and territory establishment may delay actual first reproduction for many individuals. The rapid onset of puberty is facilitated by a diet rich in flying insects, which provides the necessary protein and energy for somatic growth and the development of reproductive organs. Following puberty, the birds undergo further refinement of their flight skills and foraging efficiency before they are fully capable of sustaining the energetic demands of courtship, nesting, and parental care.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Common nighthawks is approximately 84 grams [Wwi = approximately 84 grams], representing a substantial increase from the neonatal mass and indicative of the species' moderate body size within the Caprimulgidae family. This maximum adult body mass is achieved after the completion of skeletal growth and the full development of flight musculature, which are necessary for the species' highly aerial lifestyle. Remarkably, the maximum lifespan recorded for this species, measured at 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C] under field conditions, reaches 10 years [am = 10 years], a longevity that is considerable for a bird of this size and that suggests a relatively low extrinsic mortality rate once adulthood is attained. This lifespan is consistent with the pattern seen in many caprimulgids, which, despite their aerial habits and potential exposure to predators, can persist for multiple years. The combination of a moderate adult body mass and an extended lifespan underscores a life-history strategy that balances reproductive output with survival, allowing individuals to breed repeatedly over several seasons.

The annual reproductive output of the Common nighthawk is exemplified by a maximum reprod rate that translates to a clutch size of 2 eggs per nest [N_R_i = 2 eggs per nest], typically laid directly on bare ground or on gravel rooftops in urban environments. Females usually produce a single brood each year [F_R_i = single brood each year], a frequency that is constrained by the relatively long incubation and nestling periods and the energetic costs of repeated laying. When maintained at 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], the time since birth at first brood is 350 days [tR = 350 days], meaning that individuals born in one summer are physiologically capable of first reproduction by the following breeding season. This timing aligns with the species' migratory phenology, as individuals must return to their breeding grounds in late spring before initiating nesting. The biparental care system, in which both adults share incubation and chick-rearing duties, facilitates this single annual brood by distributing the energetic burden between the sexes. The combination of a two-egg clutch and a single annual nesting attempt places the Common nighthawk at the slower end of the avian life-history continuum for an insectivore of its size.
